summary: Documents Microsoft's extensions to the PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol, usually called MS-CHAP, used to authenticate users on point-to-point links. It is informational and describes a vendor's protocol rather than an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a way for a computer to ask you to prove who you are without you sending your password in the open. Microsoft made this particular version.

questions: what is the difference between chap and ms-chap
subtitle: Microsoft's variant of PPP CHAP, which lets a remote Windows user prove their identity without the server storing a clear-text password.

tldr.problem: Microsoft wanted remote Windows workstations to authenticate over PPP with the same experience as LAN users, using the hashing and encryption already used on Windows networks.
tldr.mechanism: MS-CHAP follows standard CHAP but is selected with Algorithm 0x80, uses an 8-octet challenge, a differently structured Response, error codes in the Failure message, and packets for retrying and changing passwords.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and carries an IESG note that the protocol has significant vulnerabilities; the Security Considerations warn about attacks on the password hash.

today: RFC 2433 is an Informational document, not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own IESG note warns that the protocol has significant vulnerabilities.

sections.title: What MS-CHAP Changes
sections.content:
MS-CHAP is Microsoft's dialect of the PPP Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol, described in RFC 1994, which the reader is expected to have at hand. It was created to authenticate remote Windows workstations while giving them the functionality that LAN-based users are used to.

Where possible it matches standard CHAP. The RFC lists four differences: it is enabled by negotiating CHAP Algorithm 0x80 in LCP option 3; the Response packet has a format meant for Windows NT 3.5, 3.51 and 4.0 and Windows95, which does not require the authenticator to store a clear-text or reversibly encrypted password; the authenticator controls retries and password changes; and Failure messages carry reason codes.

An IESG note at the top of the RFC says the protocol has significant vulnerabilities and that anyone planning to implement or use it should read the Security Considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: MS-CHAP is the same kind of password game as regular CHAP, but with Microsoft's own rules for the answer, for retries and for changing your password.

sections.title: Negotiating MS-CHAP and the Challenge
sections.content:
The PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) configuration is identical to standard CHAP, except that the Algorithm field is 0x80 instead of the MD5 value 0x05. A PPP implementation that does not support MS-CHAP but correctly implements LCP Config-Rej should have no problem with this non-standard option.

The Challenge packet is identical in format to the standard CHAP Challenge. Authenticators send an 8-octet challenge Value. Peers need not copy Microsoft's way of choosing the value, but the standard guidelines on randomness SHOULD be followed. Microsoft authenticators did not provide information in the Name field at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers first agree they are going to play the Microsoft version of the game. If one of them has never heard of it, it just says no thanks and they try something else.

sections.title: The Response Packet
sections.content:
The Response packet has the standard CHAP format, but its Value field is split into three parts: a 24-octet LAN Manager compatible challenge response, a 24-octet Windows NT compatible challenge response, and a 1-octet flag meaning 'use the Windows NT compatible response'.

Each response is an encoded function of the password and the received challenge. The LAN Manager form is deprecated: peers SHOULD NOT generate it, the sub-field SHOULD be zero-filled, and the flag SHOULD always be set to 1. LAN Manager passwords are limited to 14 case-insensitive OEM characters, while the Windows NT password is 0 to (theoretically) 256 case-sensitive Unicode characters, although current Windows NT versions limit passwords to 14 characters.

The Name field holds the user account name, optionally prefixed by a Windows NT domain, for example BIGCO\johndoe. Without a domain, the backslash is omitted. The Success packet is identical to the standard CHAP Success packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Your answer has two parts, an old way and a newer way of scrambling your password with the challenge. The old way is no longer wanted, so you fill it with zeros and use the new one.

sections.title: The Failure Packet and Retries
sections.content:
The Failure packet has the standard format, but its Message field is formatted text that, unlike in standard CHAP, affects the protocol: E=eeeeeeeeee R=r C=cccccccccccccccc V=vvvvvvvvvv.

  • E is a decimal error code. Implementations should handle codes not on the RFC's list gracefully.
  • R is 1 if a retry is allowed and 0 if not. When it is 1, the authenticator disables short timeouts and expects the peer to prompt the user for new credentials.
  • C is an optional new challenge as 16 hexadecimal digits. If it is absent, the resubmitted response is calculated from the previous challenge plus decimal 23 in the first octet.
  • V is the MS-CHAP version supported by the server, assumed to be 1 if missing. Because version 1 password changes are deprecated, it SHOULD always be 2 or greater.

Implementations should accept but ignore additional text they do not recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: When the answer is wrong, the server says why using a short coded note, and whether you may try again. It is like a teacher writing 'wrong, but you have one more go' on your paper.

sections.title: Changing an Expired Password
sections.content:
MS-CHAP lets a peer change the password on the account named in the previous Response. Both Change Password packets are sent only when the authenticator reports ERROR_PASSWD_EXPIRED (E=648).

The version 1 packet (Code 5, Length 72) carries encrypted LAN Manager and Windows NT old and new password hashes, a password length and flags. It is deprecated and peers SHOULD NOT transmit it. It is for use only when V is missing or equal to one.

The version 2 packet (Code 6, Length 1118) is used when the Failure message reports version 2 or greater. It carries the new password encrypted with the old NT hash in a 516-octet field, the old NT hash encrypted with the new NT hash, two deprecated LAN Manager fields that SHOULD be zero-filled, both 24-octet challenge responses computed on the new password, and a 2-octet flags field. The RFC says it is supported by Windows NT 3.51, 4.0 and recent versions of Windows 95.

The identifier in either packet is that of the Failure packet it answers plus 1. Appendix A gives pseudocode for the hash and encryption routines, and Appendix B gives example exchanges and a worked hash for the password 'MyPw'.
sections.plainLanguage: If your password has run out, you can send a new one inside a locked box that only the server can open. There is an older, leakier box and a newer one, and you should only use the newer one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authenticator SHOULD limit the number of password retries, to make brute-force guessing harder.

The challenge is sent in clear text and is encrypted using the password hash to form the response, so both passive known-plaintext and active chosen-plaintext attacks against the password hash are possible. The RFC says suitable precautions, such as frequent password changes, SHOULD be taken wherever eavesdropping is likely.

The version 1 Change Password packet is vulnerable to a passive eavesdropping attack that can easily reveal the new password hash, so it MUST NOT be sent if eavesdropping is possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the challenge travels in the open, a sneaky listener can collect clues about your password over time. Changing your password often and limiting wrong guesses helps.
